prompt.context: Our client is a large global healthcare delivery non-profit organization. Each year they make $2 billion in grants to reduce the incidence of disease in developing nations. Every year, they allocate 20% of this budget to fighting malaria. 80% of their malaria budget goes toward R&D and 20% to onsite implementation. A few facts about malaria: Approximately 50% of the world's countries are considered 'at risk', which means malaria is common among the population. The biggest problem is in Sub-Saharan Africa. In this region, the disease has a 40% incidence rate among children under the age of 5. However, children who live past the age of 5 usually acquire immunity to the disease by this stage of their life. It is early 2008, and the malaria team has just found out that for this year, and this year only, their budget will be increased by 20%.
prompt.question: These additional funds could be invested into the purchase and distribution of bed nets, or they could be used to further R&D on a malaria vaccine with a robust pipeline. The team is equally divided between these two options and has brought us in to help them decide how to invest the additional funds. Which option should they choose?

clarifying_info.q: What is the total population of Sub-Saharan Africa?
What is the average life expectancy in Sub-Saharan Africa?
clarifying_info.a: Average life expectancy is 50 years, but the population is weighted more heavily toward the 0-5 age group.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of the Sub-Saharan Africa population falls into the 0-5 age group?
clarifying_info.a: Roughly 10% of the population falls into the 0-5 age group.

clarifying_info.q: How effective are bed nets? What is their efficacy rate?
clarifying_info.a: Efficacy is 40%, which is the frequency with which they yield the desired result.

clarifying_info.q: What is the compliance rate for bed nets?
clarifying_info.a: The compliance rate is unfortunately only 50% because once they are distributed families often use them for other purposes or don't use them at all.

clarifying_info.q: How much does each bed net cost?
clarifying_info.a: They are $5 each. That includes everything — purchase from the manufacturer, shipping, and distribution.

clarifying_info.q: How long do bed nets last?
When will the vaccine be ready?
clarifying_info.a: The vaccine will be ready for launch 4 years from now.

clarifying_info.q: What is the efficacy rate of the vaccine?
clarifying_info.a: Studies show that the vaccine will have an 80% efficacy rate.

clarifying_info.q: How would the vaccine be administered and in how many doses?
clarifying_info.a: The vaccine can be taken orally and only a single pill is required.

clarifying_info.q: How much does the vaccine cost per dose?
clarifying_info.a: The cost is $30 per vaccine, but the $100M investment will only cover research and development costs. However, if we fund the research, another organization has agreed to donate an additional $150M dedicated to the production and distribution of the vaccine.

clarifying_info.q: What is the youngest age at which the vaccine can be safely administered?
clarifying_info.a: The vaccine can be administered safely when the child is as young as one year old.

framework: Calculate the additional budget available ($100M) from the 20% one-time increase applied to the malaria budget
Determine the target population at risk: Sub-Saharan Africa children aged 0-5 with 40% malaria incidence rate
Evaluate Option A — Bed Nets: number of nets purchasable, efficacy, compliance, incidence, and duration of protection
Evaluate Option B — Vaccine R&D: leveraged additional donation ($150M), number of doses, efficacy, compliance, incidence, and duration of protection (lifelong immunity multiplier)
Compare total cases averted by each option
Consider qualitative factors: mission alignment, organizational knowledge, other actors in the space

questions.prompt: How much additional funding does the malaria team have to allocate?
questions.guidance: The candidate should calculate this before evaluating options. Annual malaria budget = $2B x 20% = $400M. A 20% one-time increase = $400M x 20% = $80M. However, the casebook uses $100M (likely rounding or a slight variant reading). The intended answer is $100M additional funds.

math.setup: Total grants = $2B; malaria allocation = 20%; one-time increase = 20%
steps: Additional funds = $400M x 20% = $80M (casebook uses $100M as the working figure)

questions.prompt: What is the 0-5 year old population in Sub-Saharan Africa?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize two valid approaches: (1) ask directly for the % in 0-5 cohort, or (2) derive from life expectancy. The casebook accepts a range of 40M–80M if using the life expectancy method with the overweighting adjustment.

steps: Method 2 (life expectancy): 800M / 50 years x 5 years = 80M per cohort; but population is NOT evenly distributed — overweight yields 40M–80M range
math.answer: 80M (using direct % method) or 40M–80M (using life expectancy with overweighting)

questions.prompt: How many cases of malaria would be averted by investing $100M in bed nets?
questions.guidance: Walk through: number of nets purchasable at $5 each, then apply efficacy x compliance x incidence rate, then multiply by 2-year lifespan. Note that 20M nets covers only 25% of the 80M children aged 0-5 — candidate should flag this gap.

math.setup: Budget = $100M; cost per net = $5; efficacy = 40%; compliance = 50%; incidence = 40%; net lifespan = 2 years
steps: Cases averted per year = 20M x 40% efficacy x 50% compliance x 40% incidence = 1.6M
Total over net lifespan = 1.6M x 2 years = 3.2M cases averted

questions.prompt: How many cases of malaria would be averted by investing $100M in vaccine R&D?
questions.guidance: The $100M funds R&D only; a partner organization donates $150M for production and distribution. Candidate should probe the compliance rate — oral single-dose delivery implies near 100%. Key insight: the vaccine provides lifelong immunity, so if administered at age 1, it protects children for approximately 4 remaining years of susceptibility (ages 1-5). This multiplier is what differentiates the vaccine option.

math.setup: Partner donation = $150M; cost per vaccine = $30; efficacy = 80%; compliance = 100%; incidence = 40%; years of protection = 4 (administered at age 1, immune by age 5)
steps: Cases averted in first year = 5M x 80% efficacy x 100% compliance x 40% incidence = 1.6M
Vaccine provides lifelong protection; if given at age 1, protects for 4 remaining susceptible years
Total cases averted = 1.6M x 4 years = 6.4M (casebook states 8M — depends on exact age/year assumptions)
Casebook answer: 1.6M x 4 = ~8M cases averted (using the casebook's stated multiplier of 4 and rounding up)
math.answer: Approximately 6.4M–8M total cases of malaria averted (casebook cites ~8M)

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the quantitative comparison, what other factors should the organization consider when choosing between bed nets and the vaccine?

categories.name: Mission and Strategy Alignment
ideas: Does the option align with the organization's stated focus (R&D vs. onsite implementation)?
Does investing in the vaccine advance the organization's long-term goal of eradicating malaria vs. treating symptoms?
80% of malaria budget already goes to R&D — vaccine investment is consistent with strategic direction

categories.name: Other Actors and Ecosystem
ideas: What are peer organizations doing — is there duplication or a funding gap in bed nets?
Is the vaccine pipeline well-funded by others already?
Does the $150M partner donation represent incremental funding or would it happen anyway?

categories.name: Implementation Risk
ideas: Bed nets have proven distribution infrastructure; vaccine requires 4-year wait before any impact
What happens if the vaccine fails in clinical trials after investing $100M?
Compliance/distribution infrastructure for a new vaccine in remote Sub-Saharan regions

categories.name: Population Coverage
ideas: 20M nets covers only 25% of at-risk 0-5 children — large gap remains
Could the $100M be split across both options?
Bed nets also protect adults; vaccine as modeled only protects children 0-5

categories.name: Timing and Urgency
ideas: Bed nets deliver immediate impact (today) vs. vaccine impact delayed 4 years
Children born in the next 4 years remain unprotected under vaccine-only strategy
One-time budget increase creates urgency to allocate wisely

recommendation: Invest the $100M additional funds in vaccine R&D, because it is expected to avert approximately 6.4M–8M cases of malaria compared to 3.2M cases for bed nets — roughly 2x the impact per dollar

The $100M leverages an additional $150M from a partner donor, multiplying the effective resource base, and the vaccine's oral single-dose delivery ensures near-100% compliance — a major advantage over bed nets' 50% compliance
risks: Clinical trial failure or delay: the vaccine may not reach market in 4 years, leaving no benefit from the $100M
Coverage gap: neither option protects the full at-risk population; many children remain unprotected regardless of choice
No immediate impact: children at risk today and over the next 4 years cannot benefit from a vaccine still in development
next_steps: Assess the robustness and stage of the vaccine pipeline to quantify development risk before finalizing the recommendation
Explore whether a portion of the $100M can simultaneously fund bed nets as a bridge strategy during the 4-year development period
Evaluate whether the partner organization's $150M donation is contingent on the $100M investment or would occur regardless
